sessions.title: # Migration Validator — AI-Native Validation Architecture Enhancement You are a senior Python architect and AI/LLM engineer working on an existing project called **Migration Validator**. The project validates migrated data between a PostgreSQL source and Snowflake target. The current system: 1. Accepts database/schema/table information. 2. Extracts PostgreSQL and Snowflake metadata. 3. Uses static and AI transformation mapping. 4. Generates N read-only SQL validation queries. 5. Generates a YAML configuration/output. 6. Does NOT execute validation SQL automatically. 7. Uses a rule book containing static and learned transformation rules. Your task is to improve the architecture without unnecessarily rewriting working functionality. The objective is to make the system: * More accurate * More deterministic * More explainable * More token efficient * Less dependent on LLM calls * Better at renamed columns * Better at type transformations * Capable of learning from previous corrections * Capable of generating SQL and YAML deterministically from one canonical validation plan ============================================================ 1. CORE ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLE ============================================================ Do NOT make the LLM directly generate the final SQL or YAML. The LLM must produce a structured, validated **Canonical Validation Plan**. The application must then deterministically generate: 1. validation.sql 2. validation.yaml from that same validation plan. The architecture must be: Schema Metadata ↓ Normalization ↓ Exact Matching ↓ Fuzzy Matching ↓ Candidate Generation ↓ AI only for ambiguous cases ↓ Canonical Validation Plan ↓ SQL Generator ↓ YAML Generator Therefore: AI = reasoning and decision making Python = validation, business rules, rendering, safety, determinism User = executes generated SQL manually Before making changes: 1. Inspect the existing project structure. 2. Inspect the CLI. 3. Inspect validation_pipeline.py. 4. Inspect SQL extraction modules. 5. Inspect static mapper. 6. Inspect AI mapper. 7. Inspect SQL generator. 8. Inspect YAML generator. 9. Inspect rule_book.py. 10. Inspect rule_book_learned.json. 11. Inspect tests. 12. Understand the existing 8 validation queries. Do not blindly rewrite the project. Preserve existing working commands and behavior wherever possible. The existing commands include functionality similar to: generate rules add-rule list-models list-tables Maintain backward compatibility unless a change is absolutely necessary. Implement the following logical components: matching/ exact_matcher.py fuzzy_matcher.py candidate_matcher.py confidence.py ai/ rule_planner.py prompt_builder.py response_parser.py core/ validation_plan.py models.py rules/ rule_book.py rule_book_base.json rule_book_learned.json transformation_catalog.yaml generators/ sql_generator.py yaml_generator.py learning/ feedback.py example_store.py retrieval.py validation/ plan_validator.py If the existing project structure differs, adapt these concepts to the existing architecture rather than unnecessarily moving every file. Continue extracting metadata from: PostgreSQL information_schema and: Snowflake information_schema The metadata model should include, where available: * database * schema * table * column name * normalized column name * data type * nullable * ordinal position * precision * scale * primary-key information if available Do not expose credentials in generated output. Implement a deterministic normalization function. Example: created_at created-at createdAt CREATED_AT CREATEDAT should normalize to: createdat Similarly: customer_id CUSTOMER_ID customer-id customerId should normalize to: customerid The normalization should: * lowercase * remove underscores * remove hyphens * remove spaces * remove non-alphanumeric characters where appropriate Keep the original column name unchanged for SQL generation. Store both: original_name and: normalized_name Never use the normalized name directly as the SQL identifier. First perform deterministic matching. Matching priority: 1. Exact original-name match where appropriate 2. Exact normalized-name match 3. Explicit configured mapping Example: source: amount target: AMOUNT should be automatically matched. Do not call the LLM for obvious exact matches. Record: match_method = "exact" or: match_method = "normalized_exact" and confidence: 1.0 Add RapidFuzz or an equivalent deterministic fuzzy matching library. Use fuzzy matching only after deterministic matching fails. For every unmatched source column: 1. Compare against unmatched target columns. 2. Normalize both names. 3. Calculate a similarity score. 4. Generate a ranked candidate list. Example: source: transaction_date candidates: TRANSACTIONDATE 0.94 TRANSACTION_DT 0.71 DATE 0.69 Do not automatically accept the highest score unless the score is above a configurable high-confidence threshold. Make thresholds configurable, for example: HIGH_CONFIDENCE = 0.95 AI_REVIEW = 0.75 These values must be configurable rather than hard-coded throughout the code. Do not rely only on fuzzy name similarity. Create a confidence calculation that can consider: * name similarity * type compatibility * known transformation compatibility * source/target position * explicit mappings * learned examples * semantic evidence The implementation should make the scoring logic explainable. Example: Name similarity: 0.98 Type compatibility: 0.90 Transformation compatibility: 1.00 Final confidence: 0.97 The exact mathematical formula can be implemented cleanly and documented. Do not pretend confidence values are statistically calibrated probabilities. Call them confidence scores. For ambiguous source columns, generate a small set of candidate target columns. Do NOT send the entire target schema to the LLM when unnecessary. For example: Source: transaction_date TIMESTAMP Candidates: 1. TRANSACTIONDATE VARCHAR fuzzy_score = 0.94 2. TRANSACTION_DT VARCHAR fuzzy_score = 0.71 3. DATE VARCHAR fuzzy_score = 0.69 The AI should receive these candidates rather than hundreds of unrelated columns. This is required to reduce token consumption and improve reasoning quality. Create or improve a transformation catalog. It should describe known PostgreSQL → Snowflake transformations. Examples may include: integer → number bigint → number smallint → number numeric → number decimal → number real → float double precision → float varchar → text character varying → text character → text text → text uuid → text date → date timestamp → timestamp_ntz timestamp → varchar where the migration process intentionally converts timestamp values to text The catalog must distinguish: TYPE COMPATIBILITY from: VALIDATION TRANSFORMATION. For example: timestamp → varchar does not necessarily mean invalid migration. It may require a normalization expression for value comparison. The AI should only be called for: * ambiguous column mappings * uncertain transformations * uncertain validation rule selection * difficult semantic cases * cases explicitly requiring AI reasoning The AI must NOT generate final executable SQL. The AI must return a structured JSON Validation Plan or mapping decision. The AI should consider: 1. Source metadata 2. Target metadata 3. Candidate matches 4. Type mapping catalog 5. Transformation catalog 6. Relevant learned examples 7. Validation rule definitions The AI must not invent columns. The AI must not invent database values. The AI must not execute SQL. The AI must not modify source or target databases. Create a strongly typed internal model called: CanonicalValidationPlan It should contain information such as: * source database * source schema * source table * target database * target schema * target table * column mappings * transformation rules * validation rules * confidence * match method * warnings * ambiguities * unmatched columns Example conceptual object: { "source_table": "public.orders", "target_table": "ORDERS", "mappings": [ { "source_column": "created_at", "source_type": "timestamp", "target_column": "CREATEDAT", "target_type": "varchar", "match_method": "fuzzy_ai", "transformation_rule": "timestamp_to_text", "confidence": 0.97, "reason": "Normalized names strongly correspond and the type difference is compatible with a known timestamp-to-text migration transformation." } ], "validation_rules": [ "row_count", "null_consistency", "duplicate_key", "missing_key", "value_integrity" ] } The exact schema should be implemented using a robust validation model, preferably Pydantic if appropriate for the existing project. Before generating SQL: Validate the CanonicalValidationPlan. Check: 1. Source table exists in extracted metadata. 2. Target table exists in extracted metadata. 3. Source columns exist. 4. Target columns exist. 5. Transformation rules are known. 6. Validation rules are known. 7. Required fields are present. 8. Confidence values are within valid ranges. 9. No source column maps to multiple targets unless explicitly allowed. 10. No target column is mapped from multiple sources unless explicitly allowed. 11. Ambiguous mappings are not silently accepted. If the plan is invalid: DO NOT generate SQL. Return a clear validation-plan error. Generate SQL deterministically from the CanonicalValidationPlan. Do not ask the LLM to write final SQL. Implement reusable SQL templates for the existing validation checks. At minimum preserve the project's existing validation capabilities: 1. Row completeness / row count 2. NULL consistency 3. Duplicate key detection 4. Missing source rows in target 5. Missing target rows relative to source where appropriate 6. Value integrity 7. Type/transformation-aware comparison 8. Aggregate or additional consistency check currently supported The generated SQL must be READ-ONLY. Never generate: INSERT UPDATE DELETE DROP ALTER TRUNCATE unless a future explicit feature specifically requires them. This is critical. Do not blindly compare: source_value = target_value when the source and target representation differs. Instead: source_value ↓ normalization/transformation ↓ comparison ↓ target_value Example: timestamp → varchar must use the transformation expression defined by the transformation catalog. The transformation expression must be generated by deterministic Python code. The LLM selects the transformation rule. The SQL generator applies the known transformation template. Do not ask the LLM to generate final YAML. Generate YAML deterministically from the same CanonicalValidationPlan used for SQL generation. The YAML should contain: * source information * target information * mappings * source/target types * transformation rules * validation rules * confidence * match method * warnings * generation metadata if useful The SQL and YAML must represent exactly the same validation plan. Improve: rule_book_learned.json The learning system must store corrections made by users. Example: { "source_column": "amount", "source_type": "numeric", "target_column": "AMOUNT", "target_type": "varchar", "previous_rule": "text", "correct_rule": "numeric", "reason": "Previous rule caused an incorrect validation comparison." } Do not blindly inject the entire learning file into every prompt. Retrieve only relevant examples. Relevant factors can include: * source column name * normalized source name * target column name * source type * target type * previous rule * transformation type Start with deterministic filtering. A future implementation may use embeddings/vector retrieval. Use this priority order: 1. Explicit user configuration 2. Static transformation rules 3. Exact/normalized matches 4. High-confidence deterministic matches 5. Relevant learned examples 6. AI semantic reasoning A learned example must NOT override an explicit configuration. AI must NOT override explicit configuration. After the user executes validation SQL and identifies a mismatch, provide a feedback workflow. Example: Mismatch detected. Was this caused by incorrect rule assignment? [Y] Yes [N] No If Yes: Ask for the correct rule. Then save a structured learning example. The system should not automatically rewrite the rule book merely because a SQL query produced a mismatch. A mismatch can be caused by: * bad source data * bad target data * incomplete migration * incorrect join/key * incorrect transformation * incorrect rule assignment * legitimate business transformation Therefore classify the feedback explicitly. Organize AI responsibilities into logical skills. Suggested skills: 1. Schema Analysis Skill 2. Column Matching Skill 3. Transformation Detection Skill 4. Validation Rule Selection Skill 5. Validation Plan Skill 6. Mismatch Analysis Skill 7. Learning Skill Skills should be modular. Do not create unnecessary LLM calls. Where deterministic logic can solve the problem, use deterministic logic. The AI system prompt must enforce: * read-only validation * structured JSON output * no SQL execution * no data modification * no invented columns * no invented transformations * evidence-based reasoning * explicit ambiguity * confidence score * reason for decision * consideration of learned examples The AI should prefer: exact evidence over fuzzy evidence over learned evidence over semantic inference. If evidence is insufficient, it must return: ambiguous rather than guessing. Use a strict structured response. Conceptually: { "status": "resolved|partial|ambiguous", "mappings": [ { "source_column": "...", "target_column": "...", "source_type": "...", "target_type": "...", "match_method": "exact|normalized|fuzzy|learned|ai|fuzzy_ai", "transformation_rule": "...", "validation_rules": [], "confidence": 0.0, "reason": "..." } ], "unmatched_source_columns": [], "unmatched_target_columns": [], "ambiguities": [], "warnings": [] } Ensure the response is parsed and validated before being accepted. The AI prompt should NOT contain: * unrelated columns * entire schemas when unnecessary * irrelevant learned examples * redundant documentation * complete rule books when only a few rules apply Send: 1. Current ambiguous source column 2. Top candidate target columns 3. Relevant source/target types 4. Relevant transformation rules 5. Relevant validation rules 6. Top relevant learned examples 7. Minimal required context This is a major requirement. Every AI-assisted mapping should expose: * source column * target column * source type * target type * match method * fuzzy score if available * transformation rule * confidence * reason * learned example used, if any This information should be visible in YAML and/or CLI output. Example: created_at → CREATEDAT Method: fuzzy_ai Name similarity: 0.98 Transformation: timestamp_to_text Confidence: 0.97 Reason: Normalized source and target names strongly correspond and the target VARCHAR representation is compatible with the configured timestamp-to-text transformation. Preserve existing CLI commands. Improve the generate command so that it can display a concise pipeline: [1/8] Extracting PostgreSQL metadata... [2/8] Extracting Snowflake metadata... [3/8] Normalizing column names... [4/8] Performing exact matches... [5/8] Performing fuzzy matching... [6/8] Resolving ambiguous mappings with AI... [7/8] Building validation plan... [8/8] Generating SQL and YAML... At the end show: Source table: public.orders Target table: ORDERS Columns: 150 source 150 target Exact matches: 132 Fuzzy matches: 12 AI-resolved: 5 Unmatched: 1 Validation rules: 8 SQL: validation_sql/orders_validation.sql YAML: validation_sql/orders_validation.yaml AI calls: 5 This makes the system's efficiency measurable. Track, where practical: * number of columns * exact matches * fuzzy matches * AI-resolved mappings * unmatched columns * AI calls * prompt token usage if available * response token usage if available * estimated cost if the model API provides usage information * generation time The goal is to demonstrate that deterministic preprocessing reduces AI usage. The validator must remain read-only. Never automatically execute generated SQL. Never automatically modify PostgreSQL. Never automatically modify Snowflake. Never expose secrets in logs. Never include database passwords or API keys in AI prompts. Never place credentials in generated SQL or YAML. Add unit tests for: 1. Name normalization 2. Exact matching 3. Fuzzy matching 4. Confidence scoring 5. Candidate generation 6. Transformation selection 7. Validation-plan validation 8. SQL generation 9. YAML generation 10. Learned-rule retrieval 11. Feedback storage Create specific regression tests for: created_at → CREATEDAT customer_id → CUSTOMERID transaction_date → TRANSACTIONDATE numeric → NUMBER timestamp → VARCHAR and other transformations already supported by the project. The following must work: SOURCE: PostgreSQL column: created_at type: timestamp TARGET: Snowflake column: CREATEDAT type: VARCHAR Expected behavior: 1. Normalize names. 2. Detect strong similarity. 3. Recognize timestamp-to-text as a possible configured transformation. 4. Avoid treating the type difference alone as a failure. 5. Resolve the mapping. 6. Produce a transformation-aware validation rule. 7. Create the canonical validation plan. 8. Generate SQL from that plan. 9. Generate YAML from that same plan. 10. Do not execute the SQL automatically. Existing static mapping behavior should continue to work. Existing rule book behavior should continue to work. Existing CLI commands should continue to work. Existing output should remain compatible where practical. Add the new architecture incrementally. Do not remove existing functionality without a clear reason. Implement in this order: STEP 1 Inspect the existing codebase. STEP 2 Create/introduce normalized metadata models. STEP 3 Implement deterministic column-name normalization. STEP 4 Implement exact matching. STEP 5 Implement RapidFuzz-based candidate matching. STEP 6 Implement confidence scoring. STEP 7 Implement candidate filtering. STEP 8 Create the CanonicalValidationPlan model. STEP 9 Implement the AI Rule Planner. STEP 10 Move final SQL generation to deterministic templates. STEP 11 Move final YAML generation to deterministic rendering. STEP 12 Implement plan validation. STEP 13 Implement learned-rule retrieval. STEP 14 Implement mismatch feedback. STEP 15 Add regression tests. STEP 16 Improve CLI output and AI usage metrics. Do not attempt all steps as one untestable rewrite. After each major step, run the relevant tests. The system should follow this principle everywhere: "Use code for what can be deterministic. Use fuzzy matching for what can be probabilistically ranked. Use AI only for what requires reasoning. Use a canonical plan as the single source of truth. Generate SQL and YAML deterministically from that plan. Learn only from explicit user feedback." The final result should be an AI-assisted PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake Migration Validator that is efficient, explainable, testable, read-only, and capable of improving its mapping decisions over time. Before implementing, inspect the existing project and explain: 1. Current architecture 2. Files that need modification 3. Files that should be added 4. Existing functionality that can be reused 5. Potential backward-compatibility risks Then implement the changes incrementally. Everything you do keep detailed documentation ready to understandable to me what we did Everything at every step
